courses.subtitle: Technology basics
courses.pitch: Try things, build and invent something of your own. You learn 3D printing, electronics, programming and robotics by doing.
topics: Getting to know the equipment and working safely
goals: work safely in Ahjo and use its equipment as you were introduced to it
model objects to measure and make them with a 3D printer
build simple circuits and measure them with a multimeter
program a microcontroller and use sensors and actuators
program and test a simple robot
document your work and assess how well it succeeded

lessons.title: Welcome to Ahjo
lessons.text: The space, the equipment and how we work; the rules and the general induction.
lessons.start: Connect an LED to a coin cell and it lights up. Turn the LED round and see what happens.

levels.try: Make the LED light and explain why it lights only one way round.
levels.modify: Change how the light looks with a ping-pong ball, paper, foil or a plastic bottle, and pick your favourite.
levels.challenge: Walk round Ahjo and record one real problem you would like to solve during the course.

lessons.output: A working light in its own cover and the first entry in the project journal.
lessons.output_plus: A recorded real problem you would like to solve during the course.
needs: ping-pong ball, paper, foil or a plastic bottle
lessons.peer: Show your light to the person next to you. Try whose shell spreads the light most evenly, and swap one idea.
lessons.goal: You recognise the parts of a circuit and why an LED works only one way round.
lessons.safety_note: A coin cell is dangerous if swallowed. Keep it on the table, never put it in your mouth and give it back to the teacher at the end of the lesson. Do not join the cell's terminals with metal, as the cell can heat up.

lessons.title: Working safely
lessons.text: The general space induction, the Makerspace licence and device induction for the 3D printer and hand tools; protective equipment and an orderly workstation.
lessons.start: Find five things in the space that have to do with safety, such as the fire extinguisher, the first aid kit and safety glasses, and photograph them.

levels.try: Take the device induction for the 3D printer and the hand tools. The induction does not yet allow you to use a device on your own: the teacher tells you what you may do.
levels.modify: Make an illustrated instruction card for one device in your own style, for example as a drawing or a comic.
levels.challenge: Write a risk assessment for the device: the hazard, how likely it is, the consequence and how to protect yourself.

lessons.output: The device induction done and an illustrated instruction card for one device.
lessons.output_plus: A risk assessment of the device.
lessons.goal: You know Ahjo's rules and how the space induction, the Makerspace licence and a device permit differ.

lessons.title: Basics of 3D modelling
lessons.text: Basic shapes, joining and holes in Tinkercad.
lessons.start: Import the key fob base from the teacher into Tinkercad and write your name on it. Your first model is done.

levels.try: Finish the key ring and save it as an STL file in the print queue.
levels.modify: Make the shape your own: add your own symbol or pattern and move the hole.
levels.challenge: Model something that fixes or improves something in your everyday life, such as a cable holder or a pen stand.

lessons.output: Your own modified key ring as an STL file in the print queue.
lessons.output_plus: A model of an object that improves something in your everyday life.
lessons.safety_note: In this lesson you model on a computer. The teacher or a student inducted on the 3D printer prints the model later.
lessons.peer: Show your unfinished model to the person next to you and ask one question you need help with.
lessons.goal: You model an object from basic shapes and save it for printing.

lessons.title: A model to measure
lessons.text: Dimensions, clearance and fitting parts together.
lessons.start: Guess the sizes of three objects, then measure them with a calliper. Who guessed closest?

levels.try: Try the fit test the teacher has printed in advance: which ring does the pin go into snugly but without force? A ring's height tells its clearance: 3 mm is 0.1 mm and 7 mm is 0.5 mm.
levels.modify: Model a lid or plug for your own jar, pen or bottle with the clearance from the fit test. First print only a thin test ring that is ready in under 15 minutes, and correct the size if it is too tight or loose.
levels.challenge: Find out how the clearance depends on the print orientation, and present the results as a table.

lessons.output: The fit test result, your own lid or plug modelled, and its size checked with a test ring.
lessons.output_plus: A table of how the clearance depends on the print orientation.
needs: the fit test printed by the teacher
lessons.goal: You measure with a calliper and design a part with a suitable clearance.
lessons.wait: If the printer is busy, measure the diameters of the fit test's pin and holes with a calliper and work out each ring's clearance. Meanwhile check your own model's dimensions in Tinkercad, and print the test ring when the printer is free.

lessons.title: From model to print
lessons.text: Slicing in PrusaSlicer, print settings and using the printer.
lessons.start: Open a ready-made beam in PrusaSlicer and change the infill. How do the print time and the mass change?

levels.try: Print the beam with the teacher's settings. Rest its ends on two piles of books 10 cm apart, hang a bag in the middle and add water or coins until the beam bends clearly or breaks. If your own beam is not ready yet, test one the teacher printed in advance.
levels.modify: Choose the infill and print orientation yourself and give your reasons. Before the test, guess whether your beam holds more or less than the teacher's beam.
levels.challenge: Weigh the load the beam held and compare two beams: which carries more per its own mass? Show the comparison as a table.

lessons.output: A printed beam, reasoned infill and orientation, and the load test result: how much the beam carried.
lessons.output_plus: A table comparing two beams: load per own mass.
needs: a bag and water or coins
lessons.safety_note: Do not touch the printer's nozzle or bed during printing or right after it: they are hot. In the load test the beam can snap without warning. Wear safety glasses, keep the load close to the floor and your feet away from under it.
lessons.goal: You slice a model and find out how infill and print orientation affect the beam's strength.
lessons.wait: If the printer is busy, do the load test with a beam the teacher printed in advance. Meanwhile record from PrusaSlicer your own beam's print time and mass, and a guess whether it holds more or less. Your own beam is tested when it is ready.

lessons.title: Judging and fixing a print
lessons.text: The most common print defects, their causes and how to fix them.
lessons.start: Pick three failed prints from the box of mistakes, name their defects and guess the causes.

levels.try: Measure your own print with a calliper and compare it with the model.
levels.modify: Change one print setting and print the corrected version as a small test piece, for example a 20 mm cube, so that it is ready within the lesson. Measure both versions at the same points and enter them in the before and after table.
levels.challenge: Put together an illustrated guide to the class's defects: the defect, the cause and the fix.

lessons.output: A before and after comparison: measurements and a photo of both versions, and a conclusion on whether the setting change improved the print.
lessons.output_plus: An illustrated defect guide: the defect, the cause and the fix.
lessons.peer: Tell another pair about one failure and one success: what did you change and what happened?
lessons.goal: You recognise print defects and check by measuring whether a fix improved the print.
lessons.wait: If the printer is busy, measure the class's earlier test cubes at the same points and compare them with the model. Work out from the measurements which setting is worth changing, and record a prediction before your own print.
lessons.safety_note: Remove a print as the teacher shows only once the bed has cooled. Do not reach into the printer while it moves.

lessons.title: Circuits and components
lessons.text: Power source, resistor, LED and breadboard.
lessons.start: Connect an LED and a 330 Ω resistor on the breadboard as in the wiring picture and take the wires to the Arduino's 5V and GND pins. The LED lights when you plug in the USB cable. No program is needed.

levels.try: Build the circuit as in the wiring picture. Always make changes with the USB cable unplugged.
levels.modify: Add a second LED first in series and then in parallel. In parallel each LED gets its own 330 Ω resistor. In which circuit do the LEDs shine brighter, and why?
levels.challenge: Size the series resistor with Ohm's law and compare the measured current with your calculation.

lessons.output: A working LED circuit and an observation of the difference between series and parallel.
lessons.output_plus: The series resistor worked out with Ohm's law and the matching measured current.
needs: Arduino Uno and USB cable (as a power source only)
two LEDs and two 330 Ω resistors
lessons.goal: You connect an LED and a series resistor and explain the difference between series and parallel circuits.

lessons.title: Measuring with a multimeter
lessons.make: How long does the battery last?
lessons.text: Measuring voltage, current and resistance connected the right way.
lessons.start: Measure the voltage of a new and a used AA battery. Which is which?

levels.try: Connect an LED and a 330 Ω resistor to the battery holder. Measure the voltage by connecting the multimeter in parallel with the battery and the current by connecting it in series in the circuit on the mA range. Then estimate the battery life: the capacity in milliampere-hours divided by the current in milliamperes gives the hours. The result is a rough estimate, because a battery's real capacity depends on the current and the temperature, and its voltage drops as it runs down.
levels.modify: Choose a device yourself, such as an LED, a motor or a buzzer, and measure its current in different situations.
levels.challenge: Measure the current with a motor or a buzzer too and compare the estimates. Think about why the real life can differ from the estimate.

lessons.output: Voltage and current measurements with units, and a rough estimate of how many hours the battery would last.
lessons.output_plus: Estimates for several devices and a reflection on why an estimate is not an exact forecast.
needs: a new and a used AA battery
battery holder for 2 × AA with wires
lessons.goal: You measure voltage and current with a multimeter connected the right way and estimate a battery's life.
lessons.safety_note: Measure voltage by connecting the meter in parallel with the part you measure. Measure current only by connecting the meter in series in the circuit. Never connect a meter set to a current range straight across the battery's terminals: that is a short circuit and can blow the meter's fuse.

lessons.title: A first Arduino program
lessons.text: The programming environment, digital outputs and a blinking LED.
lessons.start: Move the LED circuit's wire from the 5V pin to pin 13, open the ready example Blink in the Arduino IDE and change one delay number. The LED now blinks to your beat.

levels.try: Make the LED blink with the example program.
levels.modify: Turn the blinking into a heartbeat, a lighthouse or your own name in Morse code.
levels.challenge: Program a reaction-time game with a button the teacher has wired in advance, and work out the mean and spread of the class's results.

lessons.output: A working LED program you have changed yourself: your own light rhythm.
lessons.output_plus: A reaction-time game and the mean and spread of the class's results.
lessons.peer: Show your light rhythm to a partner. Can they tell what it shows?
lessons.goal: You program an Arduino output pin and change the program's timing.

lessons.title: Sensors and inputs
lessons.text: Light-dependent resistor, voltage divider, analogue input and the serial plotter.
lessons.start: Connect a light-dependent resistor and a 10 kΩ resistor as in the wiring picture, upload the ready sketch and open the serial plotter. Cover the sensor with your hand: the curve drops at once.

levels.try: Send the sensor's readings to the serial port and save them.
levels.modify: Turn the sensor into an instrument or a light that reacts to its surroundings, for example a buzzer whose pitch rises when there is more light.
levels.challenge: Calibrate the sensor, collect a series of measurements and plot a graph with units.

lessons.output: Sensor readings in the serial plotter and your own device that reacts to the sensor.
lessons.output_plus: A calibrated series of measurements and a graph with units.
needs: buzzer or LED for the modify step
lessons.goal: You read a sensor with an analogue input and interpret the readings in the serial plotter.

lessons.title: Motors and actuators
lessons.text: Servo and DC motor; power supply and control.
lessons.start: Connect a servo and a potentiometer as in the wiring picture and open the ready example Knob in the Arduino IDE. Turn the knob: the servo follows.

levels.try: Program the servo to turn to three different angles.
levels.modify: Build a cardboard figure on the servo that waves, nods or points.
levels.challenge: Make the servo follow the light, steered by two light-dependent resistors.

lessons.output: Working servo control and your own moving figure or mechanism.
lessons.output_plus: A light-following servo.
needs: card and tape for the figure
lessons.peer: Develop another pair's figure further: add one movement and note in your project diary whose work you built on.
lessons.goal: You control a servo with a program and a potentiometer.

lessons.title: Getting the robot moving
lessons.make: A robot that carries a load
lessons.text: A ready robot base, motors, a test program, measuring speed and a load test.
lessons.start: Take a ready-assembled robot base and upload the starter test sketch to it. Try the program first with the wheels in the air, then drive the robot forwards and backwards on the floor.

levels.try: Measure the robot's speed: drive straight for a set time, measure the distance with a tape measure and work out the speed. Repeat three times and change the program's SPEED number.
levels.modify: Make a cardboard load bay for the robot. Test how many grams the robot carries one metre without the load falling or the robot stopping. Improve one thing and test again.
levels.challenge: Assemble a robot base yourself from parts as the teacher instructs, or compare three SPEED values: how do the speed and the load it carries change?

lessons.output: The speed measured three times, your own load bay and the load the robot carries one metre, before and after one improvement.
lessons.output_plus: A robot base you assembled yourself, or a table comparing three speed settings.
needs: ready-assembled Arduino robot base: Arduino Uno, two DC motors, a motor driver and a battery for the motors (in the challenge you can assemble it yourself)
the starter test sketch (check the pins for your motor driver)
cardboard and tape for the load bay
kitchen scale, tape measure and stopwatch
lessons.peer: Compare load bays with another group: whose solution carries more, and why?
lessons.goal: You program a ready robot base and measure its speed and how much it carries.
lessons.wait: If there are fewer robots than groups, design a cardboard load bay meanwhile. From the speed another group measured, work out how long a drive one metre takes, and test the calculation when the robot is free.
lessons.safety_note: Test a new program first with the robot's wheels in the air on a stand. Drive the robot on the floor in a clear area. Disconnect the motor battery when you change the wiring.

lessons.title: Programming a robot
lessons.make: A square blind, then with a sensor
lessons.text: Timed moves, measuring and a first sensor trial.
lessons.start: Change the test sketch so that the robot drives a square: straight and a turn, four times. How close to the start does it come back?

levels.try: Adjust the driving time and the turning time until the square closes. Measure three times how far from the start the robot stops.
levels.modify: Do a simple sensor trial: fit a push button to the robot's front as a bump switch and add a condition to the program that stops the robot when the button is pressed. The instructions are at the end of the test sketch.
levels.challenge: Try a distance or line sensor, if one is available, and compare over three runs how the time and the accuracy change.

lessons.output: A robot that drives a square with timed moves, the measured return accuracy and a sensor trial where the robot stops at the button.
lessons.output_plus: A comparison of the sensor-controlled run: time and accuracy over three runs.
needs: push button and two wires for the sensor trial
masking tape to mark the course and a tape measure
lessons.peer: Run another pair's program on your robot and tell them where the robot left the route.
lessons.goal: You program the robot's moves and try how a sensor changes what the robot does.
lessons.wait: If the robot is busy, write the square program in advance and work out the driving time from the speed you measured in lesson 12. Meanwhile mark the course on the floor with tape.
lessons.safety_note: Test a new program first with the robot's wheels in the air. Drive the robot on the floor in a clear area, and keep cables and feet off the course.

lessons.title: Planning the mini project
lessons.text: The problem, a measurable measure of success, a materials list and a sketch.
lessons.start: Look through the mini project options below and your own course work, and choose three ideas that excite you.

levels.try: Choose one of the mini project options below or your own idea, and record its problem, measure and materials.
levels.modify: Combine two earlier exercises from the course into a new device.
levels.challenge: Make a cardboard mock-up and try the idea on another group before building.

lessons.output: A plan approved by the teacher: the idea, the measure of success, the materials and a sketch.
lessons.output_plus: A cardboard mock-up and another group's feedback on the idea.
needs: pen and paper for the sketch
lessons.peer: Add one idea you did not choose to the class's shared idea bank. Someone else may need it.
lessons.goal: You plan a small device: the problem, the measure of success and the supplies.

lessons.title: Mini project
lessons.text: A small device of your own with the methods you have learnt and ready-made solutions: building and testing.
lessons.start: Gather the parts and get the first part working, for example a sensor or a light. If a part is waiting for the printer, build a cardboard or tape version first.

levels.try: Build a working prototype by combining the course's examples and test it with your measure of success.
levels.modify: Change your solution based on the test, test again and note what the change did. A change that fails is a good result too, when you explain it.
levels.challenge: Test the device with your measure three times, improve its weakest point and make it your own: case, colour, sound or shape.

lessons.output: One round of development: a prototype, a test with the measure, a change based on the test and a new test, with a note of what you saw. The device does not have to succeed when the round is reasoned.
lessons.output_plus: Three tests, the weakest point improved and a finished look.
lessons.peer: A short show and tell halfway through the lesson: show your unfinished device and ask one question you need help with.
lessons.goal: You build, test and improve your own device for one development round.
lessons.wait: If the printer is busy, make a cardboard or tape version of the part and test the rest of the device with it. Record what the printed part has to withstand or fit.

lessons.title: Presentation and self-assessment
lessons.text: Finishing, presenting the mini project and assessing your own learning.
lessons.start: Film a 30-second video of your device working.

levels.try: Present your device: the goal, the solution and the result.
levels.modify: Choose your own way to present: a demo, a poster, a video or an exhibition stand.
levels.challenge: Say what you would do in the next version, and assess your learning with the project journal's criteria.

lessons.output: A presentation and a completed project journal.
lessons.output_plus: A plan for the next version and a self-assessment with the project journal's criteria.
lessons.safety_note: At the show your device is close to the audience. Check that it has no hot parts, sharp edges or loose wires.
lessons.peer: Try two other people's devices and leave each one a compliment and one idea for improvement.
lessons.goal: You present your work and assess your own learning.

final.title: Mini project
final.text: In the mini project you combine techniques you have already practised and ready-made solutions into a small device of your own. You do not need to learn a new technique. Planning is done in lesson 14, building and testing in lesson 15, and lesson 16 starts with half an hour for finishing before the presentation. If you continue work you started during the course, you have more time for building. Note down ideas in the project journal during the course.
options: A lamp with your own light rhythm
An LED lantern or lamp whose cover and light rhythm you design yourself. Based on lessons 1 and 9.
A sensor instrument or light alarm
A device that plays, flickers or alarms according to a sensor reading. Based on lessons 9 and 10.
A cardboard figure or mechanism moved by a servo that reacts to a button or light. Based on lesson 11.
For example a light or temperature meter whose display or case you make yourself. Based on lessons 8 and 10.
A holder, case or spare part made to measure and tested in real use. Based on lessons 3–6.
final.own: You can also carry out your own idea once the teacher has approved the plan.

start.title: The slowest ball run
start.text: Ahjo 2 starts with a quick build where failing is part of the job. The goal is not a polished result but the courage to try, test and change direction. All the materials are worked by hand, so no device induction is needed.
steps: The teacher shows the task: build a run on which a ping-pong ball travels from the edge of the desk to the floor as slowly as possible. (2 min)
Build the first version as a group. Test as soon as the ball travels even part of the way. (15 min)
Test round: time the ball's trip with a stopwatch and tell the others what did not work. (3 min)
The teacher gives each group a user card, such as “a small child must understand the run without instructions” or “the run must fit in a shoebox”. Change the run for the user on the card. (10 min)
Debrief: what failed, what did you learn from it and what did the user card change? (5 min)
start.after: The same loop of building, testing, listening to the user and changing repeats all through Ahjo 2. Write in the project journal one thing that did not work and what you learnt from it.

lessons.title: Opening challenge and project start
lessons.text: A quick build where failing is allowed, then how Ahjo 2 runs, the teams and collecting real problems. Stage 1: the problem.
lessons.example: First build the slowest ball run (35 min, instructions above). Then collect problems that matter to you, the school or your surroundings, and look through the topics in the project bank.
lessons.output: The ball run, one recorded failure and at least five recorded problems.
lessons.safety_note: The ball run is made by hand: scissors, tape and cardboard. Ahjo's machines are not used yet.
lessons.peer: Write the problems you collected in the class's shared idea bank so that other groups can take them up too.
lessons.goal: You dare to try and fail and recognise problems worth solving.

lessons.title: Defining the problem
lessons.text: Whose problem, what need, and how success is recognised. Stage 2: the user's needs.
lessons.example: Find out what users need. Interview at least three users, or if it suits your project better, observe the situation of use or gather the need in another reasoned way, for example with a survey. In an artistic project the user can be a viewer or a listener. Write the problem as: how might we help a user group in a situation where … Add a measure of success: a number you can measure or a clear qualitative sign.
lessons.output: Problem definition and measure.
lessons.milestone: Hand-in 1: the problem and the user
needs: at least three users or a situation of use to observe
lessons.goal: You find out what the user needs and define a measure of success.

lessons.title: Ideation and choice
lessons.text: At least ten ideas and a justified choice. Stage 3: solutions.
lessons.example: Ideate through constraints: what if it cost at most €20, worked without electricity, or the user had to be able to repair it? Choose with a light decision matrix that covers sustainability, accessibility, design and cost.
lessons.output: Ideas and a decision matrix.
needs: decision matrix in the project diary
lessons.peer: Brainstorm for five minutes with another group: each group comes up with three ideas for the other's problem.
lessons.goal: You come up with several solutions and choose between them with reasons.

lessons.title: Rough prototype
lessons.text: A prototype of cardboard, tape and a ready-made circuit in one lesson. Stage 4: prototype.
lessons.example: Build the quickest possible model that tests your riskiest assumption: does the user want this, and do they understand how to use it?
lessons.output: A rough prototype and the assumption to test.
lessons.peer: Show and tell: show your unfinished prototype to another group in one minute and ask one question.
lessons.goal: You test an idea with a quick and cheap model.

lessons.title: User test 1
lessons.text: An outsider tries the prototype; observations and choosing the direction. Stages 5 and 6: testing and feedback.
lessons.example: Record observations in four groups: works, does not work, unclear, and new idea. Decide whether to continue, change or change direction.
lessons.output: Test observations and a decision on how to continue.
lessons.milestone: Hand-in 2: observations from the first user test
needs: a tester from outside the group
lessons.safety_note: Another person tries your prototype. Check first that it has no sharp edges, loose parts, bare wires or hot spots. The tester does not use Ahjo's machines.
lessons.peer: Test another group's prototype and give your findings under the same four headings.
lessons.goal: You collect observations from a user and decide on that basis how to go on.

lessons.title: Project plan
lessons.text: Milestones, roles, a priced materials list and risks.
lessons.example: Write a plan as in a real product development project: who does what and when, what the materials cost and what could go wrong.
lessons.output: Project plan and budget.
lessons.goal: You plan the division of work, the schedule, the budget and the risks.

lessons.title: Design, materials and methods
lessons.text: A plan from which someone else could build the same thing, and a justified choice of material.
lessons.example: Choose a way of designing and documenting that suits your project: a dimensioned drawing, a 3D model, a circuit diagram, a textile pattern, a flow chart or another justified way. Make it clear enough for another group to build the same part. Compare at least two materials by strength, price, production time and recyclability.
lessons.output: A plan that suits the project (for example a dimensioned drawing, a 3D model or a circuit diagram) and the choice of material.
needs: computer and a suitable design program
lessons.goal: You make a plan from which someone else could make the same part, and justify your choice of material.

lessons.title: Working prototype
lessons.text: The first working version of the solution with Ahjo's equipment.
lessons.example: Build the prototype's parts with Ahjo's machines. Share the work so that everyone takes part in making it and learns at least one thing new to them. You do not need every method: choose the ones your project really needs.
lessons.output: A working prototype.
needs: Ahjo's devices with the teacher's permission
lessons.peer: At the end of the lesson tell the other groups about one success and one failure.
lessons.goal: You make the prototype's parts with Ahjo's equipment and learn at least one new method.
lessons.wait: If the device you need is busy, first make the parts that do not need it, or make a cardboard version of the part. Start the test plan alongside.

lessons.title: Test plan and measurements
lessons.text: What is measured, how precisely and how many repetitions. Stage 6: measurement results.
lessons.example: Write a test plan and test the prototype with your measure of success three times. If the measure is a number, show the results as a table and a graph. If measuring a number does not suit the project, use a qualitative test, for example observation, a user's rating on a scale or before and after photos, and record the results just as carefully.
lessons.output: Test plan and the first results.
needs: measuring tools or an observation form
lessons.safety_note: Test your own prototype only with machines and tools you have been inducted into and the teacher has allowed. If the prototype has electricity, moving parts or heat, agree the test with the teacher before you start.
lessons.goal: You plan a test and collect results by measuring or observing.

lessons.title: User test 2
lessons.text: A user tries the working prototype without instructions.
lessons.example: Watch the user without stepping in and record where they hesitate or make a mistake. Compare with the first test.
lessons.output: Observations from the second user test.
lessons.safety_note: Another person tries your prototype. Check first that it has no sharp edges, loose parts, bare wires or hot spots. The tester does not use Ahjo's machines.
lessons.goal: You observe a user without stepping in and compare the results with the earlier test.

lessons.title: Improvement 1
lessons.text: Changes based on the tests and feedback. Stage 7: improvement.
lessons.example: Choose the two most important changes on the basis of the tests, justify them and make them.
lessons.output: Two justified changes.
lessons.peer: If another group has solved a similar problem, you may use its solution when you credit it in the project diary.
lessons.goal: You change the solution on the basis of the tests and justify the changes.

lessons.title: Improvement 2
lessons.text: An improvement whose effect shows in the measurements.
lessons.example: Choose one improvement based on the test results and test its effect with the same measure or observation as before. The improvement can be a new part or sensor, but just as well a simpler structure, a different material or a better program. If the improvement does not work, that is a valuable result too: record what you tried, what you measured and what you learned.
lessons.output: A tested improvement and its reasons, also if the improvement did not work.
lessons.goal: You test whether a change improved the solution, and learn from an improvement that failed too.

lessons.title: Final testing
lessons.text: Does the solution work: the same measures as in the test plan.
lessons.example: Test the final solution with the same measures or observations as in the test plan and judge whether you reached the goal set at the start. If you changed the solution after the previous test, test the changed part again.
lessons.output: Test report.
lessons.safety_note: Test your own prototype only with machines and tools you have been inducted into and the teacher has allowed. If the prototype has electricity, moving parts or heat, agree the test with the teacher before you start.
lessons.peer: Ask another group to try your solution. Do they find a fault you did not notice yourselves?
lessons.goal: You assess with the same measures as in the test plan whether you reached the goal.

lessons.title: Finishing and user guide
lessons.text: Last fixes, appearance and usability.
lessons.example: Finish the solution for the show: case, labels and a user guide that let the user manage without its maker. If finishing changes how it works, for example a case covers a sensor or a wire moves, check that it works again before the show.
lessons.output: A finished solution and a user guide.
needs: materials for the case and the labels
lessons.goal: You finish the solution so that the user manages without you.
lessons.wait: If the printer or another device is busy, write the user instructions meanwhile and try them out on another group.

lessons.title: Documentation
lessons.text: Project journal, materials list, editable files and sources. Stage 8: documentation.
lessons.example: Put together a one-page summary from the journal that tells your decisions and failures honestly. It also serves an upper secondary diploma and applications to further studies.
lessons.output: Summary and files.
lessons.goal: You put the project's course, decisions and failures together honestly.

lessons.title: Presentation and assessment
lessons.text: Presenting the project and assessing your own and the group's work.
lessons.example: Present the project to an audience and make a video of at most one minute. Finally, assess your own and the group's work with the project journal's criteria.
lessons.output: Presentation, video and self-assessment.
lessons.safety_note: At the show your solution is close to the audience. Check that it has no hot parts, sharp edges or loose wires.
lessons.goal: You present the project and assess your own and the group's work.

courses.flex: Projects differ, and not everyone has to make the same kind of solution. The lessons are a guiding model: the hand-ins are the same for everyone, but groups can move at different paces with the teacher's guidance. Building and testing can partly run in parallel, for example the test plan is written during a long building stage. The journal records what the group actually did.

snacks.title: Maker snacks
snacks.text: Optional 10–15 minute experiments for the middle of the project work, lessons 8–12. The teacher can bring them out when the work is stuck or a group needs a new idea. Nothing is handed in, and your own project stays the main thing.

items.title: A prototype from an odd material
items.text: Make a model of the most important part of your project from a material you have not used yet: foil, straws, clothes pegs, fabric or modelling clay. What did the new material reveal about your solution?

items.title: Mechanism try-out
items.text: Build one mechanism from cardboard that you have not tried yet: a lever, a cam, a hinge or a crank. Could it work in your project?

items.title: The ten-object challenge
items.text: The group gets a bag of random materials and in ten minutes builds from them a solution to one part of the project's problem.

items.title: Paper user interface
items.text: Draw your device's buttons, display or instructions on paper and let someone from another group try them. You act as the device and react to the presses. Where do they hesitate?

assessment.lead: The assessment is based on the project journal, the five hand-ins and the teacher's observations. The levels are described in the project journal guide. It takes into account:
items: defining the problem and the user's need
ideation and a justified choice of solution
planning and carrying out the project
documentation and showing your own skills
assessment.note: Technical flair or a successful end product alone does not decide the assessment. A failed prototype can show excellent skills when the design, the testing, the analysis of observations and the development decisions are justified. Everyone shows their own part in the hand-ins. The assessment is a draft, and the teacher decides on the weighting.

courses.subtitle: Fly, program and investigate
courses.pitch: Build a programmable drone, learn to fly it safely and investigate by measuring why it stays in the air. Finally, you carry out your own drone project.

units.title: Get to know drones and fly safely

topics: Drone structure, motors, sensors and control
The physics of flight: forces, torques and flight stability
Experimental research: measuring, repeats and sources of error
Analysing measurement data and video with Python
goals: fly a drone safely and act as pilot, observer and safety officer
explain, using forces and torques, why a quadcopter hovers, tilts and turns
assemble a programmable drone and check that it works before a flight
program a micro:bit as a radio controller and read the drone's control program
plan a flight test, repeat a measurement and assess the sources of error
process measurement data with Python and justify your conclusions with a graph
plan, build and document your own technical solution

lessons.title: Getting to know drones and flight safety
lessons.text: The parts of a drone, marking out the flight area and three roles: pilot, observer and safety officer.
lessons.start: Watch the drone flown by the teacher and write down three things that could go wrong. Compare your list with a partner.

levels.try: With your group, make a pre-flight checklist and draw the classroom flight area: the take-off spot, the safety line and the place for spectators. Practise the roles and the calls Take-off, Stop and Land without a drone.
levels.modify: Add an item to the checklist for each hazard you wrote down at the start, and test the list with another group.
levels.challenge: Find out from Traficom's Unmanned aviation (Miehittämätön ilmailu) pages what is required of someone flying a camera drone that weighs less than 250 grams. Write down three rules and the page where you found them.

lessons.output: The group's checklist and a drawing of the flight area, which are used throughout the course.
lessons.output_plus: Three rules of flying in your own words, with sources.
needs: masking tape for marking out the flight area
safety glasses for the safety officer
a drone flown by the teacher
lessons.safety_note: In this lesson only the teacher flies the drone. Stay behind the safety line when the propellers are spinning.
lessons.peer: Swap checklists with another group. Does their list have an item that your own group did not notice?
lessons.goal: You know the main parts of a drone and can act in your own role in the flight area.
diary: the group's checklist
the drawing of the flight area and the roles
one thing that surprised you

teacher.time: Start and demonstration flight 15 min, checklist and flight area 30 min, practising the roles 20 min, summary 10 min.
teacher.prep: Book a room with free floor space and agree on the use of the room with the school. Charge the batteries and check the drone. Print the safety induction guide. No devices are handed out to students in this lesson.

lessons.title: Why does a drone fly? Forces and torques
lessons.text: Weight, lift and the directions in which the propellers spin: how a quadcopter climbs, tilts and turns.
lessons.start: Cut a helicopter out of paper following the teacher's template and drop it three times. Measure the fall time with a stopwatch.

levels.try: Draw the force diagram of a hovering drone and calculate how much lift one propeller has to produce when you know the mass of the drone. Mark the directions in which the propellers spin on the diagram.
levels.modify: Change the blade length of the paper helicopter and measure the fall time with five drops. How does the blade length affect it?
levels.challenge: Explain, using forces and torques, why the drone turns about its vertical axis when two opposite propellers spin faster than the others.

lessons.output: A force diagram of a hovering drone and the calculated lift of one propeller.
lessons.output_plus: An explanation of how the drone turns, using torques.
needs: the mass of the drone (from the teacher or a scale)
lessons.safety_note: There is no flying in this lesson. The drones stay in their boxes.
lessons.peer: Compare your force diagram with your partner's. Are the lengths of the forces in the right proportion?
lessons.goal: You explain hovering as a balance of forces and tilting using torques.
diary: the force diagram and the calculation
the measurement results for the paper helicopter
which result differed from what you expected, and why

teacher.time: Paper helicopter 15 min, theory and force diagram 25 min, measurements 25 min, summary 10 min.
teacher.prep: Print the paper helicopter template and weigh one drone in advance. If necessary, revise Newton's laws and torque.

lessons.title: The structure and components of the Air:bit 2
lessons.text: Frame, control board, motors, propellers, battery and micro:bit: what each part does.
lessons.start: Open the building kit and sort the parts into groups before you read the instructions. Guess what each group is for.

levels.try: On the control board, identify the micro:bit connector, the motor connections, the battery connector and the charging connector. Draw a parts map that shows where the power and the control signals travel.
levels.modify: Work out from the propellers which way each one has to spin, and mark the directions on the parts map.
levels.challenge: Weigh the parts of the kit and calculate the mass of the whole drone. Estimate how large a share of the mass is battery, and think about why that matters.

lessons.output: A parts map with the parts of the drone and their jobs labelled.
lessons.output_plus: A table of masses and the battery's share of the drone's mass.
needs: one Air:bit 2 building kit per group
lessons.safety_note: The battery is not connected yet. Do not bend or press the battery, and tell the teacher straight away if a battery is swollen or damaged.
lessons.peer: Explain the job of one part to your partner so that they can point to it on the parts map.
lessons.goal: You name the parts of the drone and say what each of them does.
diary: the parts map
a question you do not know the answer to yet

teacher.time: Sorting 10 min, identifying the parts and parts map 35 min, propellers and weighing 20 min, summary 10 min.
teacher.prep: Check that every kit has all its parts, and number the kits and micro:bits by group. Charge the batteries ready for next time according to the manufacturer's instructions.

lessons.title: Assembling the drone and function tests
lessons.text: Assembling the frame and motors, and a start-up test without propellers.
lessons.start: Attach one motor to the frame according to the instructions and show it to the teacher. Carry on only after that.

levels.try: Assemble the drone according to the instructions, but leave the propellers off. Start the drone on a level surface and record which letters the micro:bit display shows during start-up.
levels.modify: Do the motor test without propellers and check from your parts map that every motor is in the right place.
levels.challenge: Write a troubleshooting card: what do you do if the display reports that the gyroscope or the motor controller cannot be found?

lessons.output: An assembled drone that starts up and passes the motor test without propellers.
lessons.output_plus: A troubleshooting card for two start-up errors.
lessons.safety_note: The propellers are not attached in this lesson. The battery is connected only after the teacher has checked the assembly.
lessons.wait: While you wait for the teacher's check, add to your parts map or help another group read the instructions.
lessons.peer: Check another group's drone using the checklist before the teacher looks at it.
lessons.goal: You assemble a drone according to the instructions and test safely that it works.
diary: a photo of the assembled drone
the start-up stages and the symbols on the display
what was hardest about the assembly

teacher.time: First motor 10 min, assembly 40 min, start-up and motor test 15 min, summary 10 min. Allow extra time if needed: the manufacturer estimates 2–3 hours for assembly.
teacher.prep: Charge the batteries. Load the drone program onto the micro:bits in advance or allow time for it. In the manufacturer's instructions the propellers are attached at the end of the assembly chapter: skip that step and keep the propellers yourself until the flying lessons.

lessons.title: micro:bit, MakeCode and radio control
lessons.text: Two micro:bits communicate by radio: one is the controller, the other receives.
lessons.start: Load onto the micro:bit a program that sends a number by radio when you press button A. Try with your partner's micro:bit whether the number arrives.

levels.try: Program the micro:bit to send its tilt and the state of the buttons by radio as named values. Show on the receiving micro:bit that the values change when you tilt the controller.
levels.modify: Change the radio group to your group's own and add throttle control to the controller with buttons A and B so that the value stays between 0 and 100.
levels.challenge: Add a safety feature: the controller sends permission to start only when A and B are pressed at the same time, and shows the state clearly.

lessons.output: A controller program that sends tilt and throttle by radio on the group's own channel.
lessons.output_plus: A controller with a two-button start safeguard.
needs: a battery holder for the controller
lessons.safety_note: In this lesson you program and test on the desk. The drone's battery is not connected.
lessons.peer: Try your partner's controller and tell them one thing that would make it easier to use.
lessons.goal: You program a micro:bit to send control commands by radio.
diary: a screenshot of the program
the number of the group's radio group
how you tested that the message gets through

teacher.time: First radio message 10 min, controller program 40 min, radio groups and throttle 15 min, summary 10 min. The manufacturer estimates 3–4 hours for programming the controller, so the work continues next time.
teacher.prep: Give each group its own radio group number. Keep the manufacturer's ready-made controller program in reserve for groups whose own program is not finished.

lessons.title: Studying and modifying the drone's control program
lessons.text: How the drone program reads the sensors, calculates the attitude and shares the power between four motors.
lessons.start: Open the drone's program in MakeCode and find the place where the radio message is received. Which five values does the controller send?

levels.try: Follow the main loop of the program and make a reading map: reading the sensors, calculating the attitude, control and the motor speeds. Mark the place where the motors are stopped for safety reasons.
levels.modify: Change something that does not affect flight: for example what is shown on the display or when the battery warning appears. Test the change without propellers.
levels.challenge: Explain from the formula for the motor speeds why, when tilting forwards, the power of two motors increases and that of two decreases.

lessons.output: A reading map of the stages and safety functions of the drone program.
lessons.output_plus: An explanation of how the program shares the power between four motors.
lessons.safety_note: All changes are tested without propellers. Values that affect flight are not changed yet.
lessons.wait: If the computer or the drone is in use, finish your controller program or write up a clean copy of the reading map.
lessons.peer: Explain one stage of your reading map to your partner. Your partner asks one question, and you look for the answer in the program together.
lessons.goal: You read a ready-made program and say what its parts do.
diary: the reading map
the change you made and how you tested it
a part of the program you do not understand yet

teacher.time: Finding the radio handler 10 min, reading map 35 min, own change and test 20 min, summary 10 min.
teacher.prep: Make sure that the drone program opens in MakeCode on the school's computers. Save a copy of the original program so that it can be restored.

lessons.title: First flight tests with the Air:bit 2
lessons.text: Checklist, calibration and short hovers in a marked-out flight area.
lessons.start: Go through the group's checklist aloud and share out the roles: pilot, safety officer and recorder. Show the list to the teacher before the propellers are attached.

levels.try: Attach the propellers under the teacher's supervision and let the drone calibrate while standing still on a level surface. Do three short hovers: raise the throttle one step at a time until the drone hovers at a height of 10–30 cm. For each flight, record the duration and the direction in which the drone drifted.
levels.modify: Swap roles and repeat the test. Did the direction of the drift change when the pilot changed or when the drone was calibrated again?
levels.challenge: Plan a test to find out whether the drift is caused by the drone or by the pilot. Write down what you keep constant and what you change.

lessons.output: A flight log of three hovers: duration, drift and observations.
lessons.output_plus: A test plan for finding the cause of the drift.
needs: a micro:bit programmed as the controller
a soft surface, for example a rug, on the floor of the flight area
lessons.safety_note: The drone has no altitude hold or position hold: the pilot controls the height the whole time. You fly low over a soft surface, one drone at a time in the flight area. The emergency stop is shaking the controller, and it is tried out before the propellers are attached.
lessons.wait: While another group is flying, act as recorder or measure the duration of their hover from video.
lessons.peer: Give the pilot one compliment and one piece of advice after each flight.
lessons.goal: You carry out the pre-flight checks and fly the drone briefly and under control.
diary: the flight log
which checklist item was the most important
what you would change next time

teacher.time: Checklist and roles 10 min, propellers and calibration 15 min, flying turns 40 min, summary 10 min.
teacher.prep: Check the flying space and mark out the flight area. Charge the batteries and have spare propellers ready. Decide how long the flying turns are and how many drones are running at once. Approve each group's checklist before the flight.

lessons.title: Investigating flight stability and developing the program
lessons.text: How the values of the feedback controller affect how steadily the drone hovers.
lessons.start: Look in last time's flight log to see how much the drone drifted. Set a target for the group: what would a steadier hover mean, and how would you measure it?

levels.try: Do a comparison test with the original tuning values: three hovers, for each of which you measure the drift from the starting point in a set time. Calculate the mean and the range.
levels.modify: With the teacher's permission, change one tuning value in small steps and repeat the same test. Record the value before and after. Restore the original value if the drone starts to wobble.
levels.challenge: Use your observations to explain what the gain of the feedback controller does: why does too small a value make the drone sluggish and too large a value make it oscillate?

lessons.output: The results of the comparison test: the mean and range of the drift with the original values.
lessons.output_plus: A second series of measurements with a changed value and a justified conclusion.
needs: an Air:bit 2 in flying condition and a controller
a starting point taped on the floor
lessons.safety_note: Tuning values are changed one at a time and only within the limits approved by the teacher. A changed program is tested first without propellers.
lessons.wait: While the drone is with another group, enter your measurements in a table and calculate the means.
lessons.peer: Compare your results with another group's. Did you measure the drift in the same way?
lessons.goal: You do a comparison test and use measurements to justify whether the flight stability improved.
diary: the test set-up and what you kept constant
the table of measurements and the means
the changed values and the original values

teacher.time: Target and test set-up 15 min, comparison test 25 min, change and repeat test 25 min, summary 10 min.
teacher.prep: Decide in advance which values may be changed and by how much. Save the original program for each group. Charge the batteries: flight time affects the results, so agree that the measurements are made with a full battery. The manufacturer's instructions do not include changing the tuning values, so the task is the school's own: try it yourself before the lesson.

lessons.title: The basics of FPV flying
lessons.text: You fly a camera drone with goggles and a motion controller in Normal mode. The observer stands next to the pilot.
lessons.start: Hold the motion controller in your hand with the device switched off and practise the movements the teacher shows: braking and hovering, climbing, turning and landing.

levels.try: At the station, do one FPV flight: take-off, hover, a slow flight to the marker and back, and landing. Also act once as observer and once as safety officer.
levels.modify: Fly the same route without goggles, looking straight at the drone. Which way was more accurate, and why?
levels.challenge: Describe what information the view in the goggles gives the pilot and what information only the observer sees.

lessons.output: One controlled FPV flight and experience of each of the three roles.
lessons.output_plus: A comparison between FPV flight and direct line of sight.
needs: a camera drone with propeller guards
FPV goggles and a motion controller
safety glasses for the safety officer
lessons.safety_note: With the goggles on you cannot see around you. The observer stands next to you, keeps the drone in sight the whole time without any aids and says Stop if anything comes into the flight area. You fly only in Normal mode. Stop immediately if you start to feel dizzy or unwell.
lessons.wait: When it is not your turn to fly, practise the control movements with the controller switched off, or plan the precision course for next time.
lessons.peer: After the flight, the observer tells the pilot one thing that the pilot did not see through the goggles.
lessons.goal: You fly an FPV drone under control and act as observer.
diary: the roles you acted in
how FPV flight felt compared with direct line of sight
the observer's observations

teacher.time: Control movements and rules 15 min, stations 50 min, summary 10 min. With two drones, a group of about four students per station has time to fly.
teacher.prep: Read the device's user manual and safety instructions. The manufacturer states that the product is not intended for children and does not give an age limit: the school decides on its use in teaching. Check who the registered user (operator) is and that the ID is marked on the drones. Agree on the use of the room and on the rules for filming. Attach the propeller guards, charge the batteries and make sure that the flying space is well lit and roomy: in a cramped or dim space the drone can lose its positioning and drift. Sport mode and Easy ACRO tricks are not used, because obstacle avoidance is switched off in them. Clean the goggles between users. Arrange a parallel task for the rest of the group.

lessons.title: Precision flight test and measuring the flight path
lessons.make: A series of precision landing measurements
lessons.text: How accurately does a landing hit the mark, and how much do the results vary?
lessons.start: Tape a landing mark on the floor and agree in your group which point the landing accuracy is measured from. Write the rule down before the first flight.

levels.try: Fly from the starting point to the mark and land five times. Measure the distance of each landing from the centre of the mark and record the results in a table.
levels.modify: Change one thing, for example the starting distance or the pilot, and repeat the series of five landings. Keep everything else the same.
levels.challenge: Film the flight from the side with a phone on a tripod and measure from the video the flight time from take-off to landing. Calculate the drone's average speed.

lessons.output: A table of measurements for five landings and their mean.
lessons.output_plus: A second series of measurements in which one thing has been changed, or the average speed calculated from video.
needs: a camera drone with propeller guards and a controller
a phone and a tripod for filming
safety glasses for the safety officer
lessons.safety_note: Only the flight area and the drone are filmed. Nobody is filmed without permission, and the videos are not published.
lessons.wait: While the drone is with another group, measure and record their landings or enter your own results in the table.
lessons.peer: Another group measures one of your landings. Do you get the same result?
lessons.goal: You repeat a measurement and describe the variation in the results with the mean and the range.
diary: the measuring rule and the test set-up
the table of measurements
the biggest source of error and how you would reduce it

teacher.time: Test set-up and measuring rule 15 min, series of measurements at the stations 45 min, recording the results and summary 15 min.
teacher.prep: Mark out two flight areas if there is enough room. Have tape measures and a tripod ready. Remind students of the rules for filming. The rest of the group can measure Air:bit hovers or analyse earlier data.

lessons.title: Analysing flight video and measurement data with Python
lessons.make: A graph of your own measurement data
lessons.text: Measurements from a table into Python: mean, spread and a graph that shows the conclusion.
lessons.start: Run the ready-made Python program with the example data and see what graph it draws. Then replace the data with your own group's measurement file.

levels.try: Read your group's measurements from a file, calculate the mean and the standard deviation and draw a graph that shows all the measurements and the mean.
levels.modify: Compare two series of measurements in the same graph and write one sentence on whether the difference is bigger than the variation in the measurements.
levels.challenge: Measure the drone's position from a few frames of the video and calculate the speed at different moments. Compare the result with the average speed obtained with a stopwatch.

lessons.output: A graph of your own measurement data, and the mean and standard deviation.
lessons.output_plus: A comparison of two series of measurements, or a speed measured from video.
needs: a Raspberry Pi or another computer with Python
lessons.safety_note: There is no flying in this lesson. Handle the videos only on the school's devices, and do not share them with anyone.
lessons.wait: If the computer is in use, check your table of measurements: does every number have a unit, and are the outlying values marked?
lessons.peer: Show your graph to your partner without explaining it. What do they conclude from it?
lessons.goal: You process measurement data with Python and justify a conclusion with a graph.
diary: the graph and the statistics
the conclusion in one sentence
what you would measure differently

teacher.time: Ready-made program and example data 15 min, own data and graph 35 min, comparison or video 15 min, summary 10 min.
teacher.prep: Install Python and the plotting library on the computers and try out the starter program. Collect the groups' measurement files in one folder. Video analysis requires a video in which the camera stays still and a scale is visible in the picture.

lessons.title: Drone control engineering and comparing the flight tests
lessons.text: Feedback: the sensor measures, the program compares and the motors correct. The results of the flight tests are brought together.
lessons.start: Hold the drone in your hand without propellers and tilt it slowly. Use the motor test or the display to see in which direction the program tries to correct.

levels.try: Draw the drone's control loop as a block diagram: target attitude, sensors, feedback controller, motors and drone. Attach the results of your group's stability test to the diagram.
levels.modify: Compare the stability results of at least two groups and explain what the differences could be due to: the drone, the battery, the pilot or the way of measuring.
levels.challenge: Do a second control test with a different value from the one in lesson 8 and plot the results in the same graph as the earlier ones. With which value was the hover steadiest?

lessons.output: A block diagram of the drone's control loop and a summary of the results of the stability test.
lessons.output_plus: A graph comparing at least two tuning values.
needs: charged batteries and safety glasses, if you fly
lessons.safety_note: The hand-held test is always done without propellers. In a flight test the same limits apply as in lesson 8.
lessons.wait: If the drone is in use, finish the block diagram and write the summary of the results.
lessons.peer: Explain your block diagram to your partner by following one loop with your finger: what happens when the wind tilts the drone?
lessons.goal: You describe the stabilisation of the drone as feedback and compare test results.
diary: the block diagram
the summary of the results and the graph
an idea for your own project

teacher.time: Hand-held test 10 min, block diagram 25 min, comparing the results or a second control test 30 min, summary 10 min.
teacher.prep: Collect the groups' stability results in one table. Decide whether there is flying this time. At the end, introduce the project bank for next time.

lessons.title: Coming up with and planning your own project
lessons.text: You choose a topic from the project bank or your own idea and write a plan whose success can be measured.
lessons.start: Read the cards in the project bank and choose the two most interesting ones. For each, write one question that the project would answer.

levels.try: Write the group's project plan: the research question or problem, the equipment needed, the work stages, a measurable success criterion and safety. Get the teacher to approve the plan.
levels.modify: Add a back-up plan to the plan: what do you do if a device is in use or the first solution does not work?
levels.challenge: Propose a project of your own that is not in the bank. Justify why it can be done with the school's equipment and how its success is measured.

lessons.output: A project plan approved by the teacher, with a measurable success criterion.
lessons.output_plus: A back-up plan, or a justified project idea of your own.
lessons.safety_note: A project that involves flying is not started until the teacher has approved the safety section of the plan.
lessons.peer: Present the plan to another group in two minutes. They ask: how do you know that you have succeeded?
lessons.goal: You define a project whose success can be measured.
diary: the project plan
the success criterion
the division of work and a schedule for three sessions

teacher.time: Project bank 15 min, plan 40 min, presentation to another group 10 min, approvals 10 min.
teacher.prep: Check which projects can be done with the current equipment and which require an additional purchase. Allow time for approving the plans and for making the equipment booking list.

lessons.title: Building and programming the project
lessons.text: The project is built or programmed far enough that it can be tried out.
lessons.start: Read this session's target from the plan and share out the work. Every member of the group has a task during the first five minutes.

levels.try: Build or program the first version of the project and do one test with it, even if not everything works yet. Record what happened.
levels.modify: Improve one thing on the basis of the first test and record what you changed and why.
levels.challenge: Prepare a measurement for next time: make a table for the measurements and decide how many repeats are needed.

lessons.output: The first version of the project and a record of the first test.
lessons.output_plus: One justified improvement, or a finished measurement plan.
needs: the equipment listed in the project plan
lessons.safety_note: Follow the safety section of your plan. If the plan changes so that you fly in a different way, ask for a new approval.
lessons.wait: If the device you need is in use, work on another part of the project: the table for the measurements, the 3D model or the documentation.
lessons.peer: Show your unfinished work to another group and ask one question that you need help with.
lessons.goal: You build the first version of your plan and try it out.
diary: what was done and who did it
the result of the first test
the target for next time

teacher.time: Sharing out the work 5 min, building and programming 55 min, diary and tidying up 15 min.
teacher.prep: Make an equipment booking list from the groups' plans. Charge the batteries. Agree where the groups that fly will work, and when.

lessons.title: Testing and improving the project
lessons.make: Measurement results and an improved version
lessons.text: The project is tested by measuring, improved and tested again.
lessons.start: Read your success criterion aloud and straight away make one measurement that tells you how far you are from it.

levels.try: Carry out the planned series of measurements, record the results and compare them with the success criterion. Make one change and measure again.
levels.modify: Draw a graph of the results before and after the change and write whether the change improved the result.
levels.challenge: Assess the biggest source of error in your measurements and suggest how it could be reduced.

lessons.output: Measurement results before and after one change. An unsuccessful change is also accepted when it has been measured and justified.
lessons.output_plus: A graph of the results, or an assessment of the sources of error.
lessons.safety_note: A changed drone or program is tested first without propellers or at low height, as in earlier lessons.
lessons.wait: If the device is in use, process the data you have already collected and start putting the presentation together.
lessons.peer: Another group repeats one of your measurements. What causes the difference between their result and yours?
lessons.goal: You test your solution by measuring and improve it on the basis of the results.
diary: the measurement results and the graph
the change you made and its effect
what you would do if there were more time

teacher.time: First measurement 10 min, series of measurements 25 min, change and new measurement 25 min, diary 15 min.
teacher.prep: Have measuring instruments ready and book flying turns. Remind students that what counts in the assessment is measured and justified development, not just a working end result.

lessons.title: Drone Challenge, presentation and self-assessment
lessons.text: The projects are presented, the shared Drone Challenge is flown and you assess your own work.
lessons.start: Put your project on display and write one sentence on a card: what you investigated or solved and what the most important result was.

levels.try: Present the project: the problem, the solution, the measurement results and what you learned. Answer one question and fill in the self-assessment.
levels.modify: Take part in the Drone Challenge with your group in the role you have chosen and record the group's result.
levels.challenge: Write a proposal for further development: what could the next group do with your project?

lessons.output: A presented project, a finished project diary and a self-assessment.
lessons.output_plus: A Drone Challenge result, or a proposal for further development.
needs: the Drone Challenge course and equipment
lessons.safety_note: There are spectators at the Drone Challenge: they stay behind the safety line, and every flight has a named observer and safety officer.
lessons.peer: Give each presentation one question or compliment on a card.
lessons.goal: You present the results of your project and assess your own work.
diary: the main points of the presentation
the feedback you received
the self-assessment

teacher.time: Exhibition and presentations 35 min, Drone Challenge 25 min, self-assessment and feedback 15 min.
teacher.prep: Build the Drone Challenge course and mark out the spectators' area. Print the self-assessment forms. Decide which tasks are flown on the course: precision landing is achievable for everyone, the obstacle course requires more flying experience.

final.title: Drone Challenge
final.text: At the end of the course, every group presents its own project and takes part in the shared Drone Challenge. The tasks are chosen so that every group can succeed at its own level.
options: Five landings on the mark. The result is the mean of the distances, not the best single hit.
A lap through a marked course following the observer's instructions. The result is the time and the number of touches.
The Air:bit stays inside a marked area for as long as possible.
The group presents a measurement result whose reliability it can justify.
final.own: You can propose a task of your own once the teacher has approved its rules and safety.

assessment.lead: The assessment is based on what you produce in the lessons, the project diary, the project and the teacher's observations. The assessment takes into account:
items: safe and responsible conduct in all roles
understanding of the programming and the technical implementation
analysis of measurement results and justification of conclusions
development based on feedback and measurements
assessment.note: Good flying skill alone does not decide the assessment. A failed prototype can also show excellent skills when the work is systematic, tested and documented with justification. The scope of 2 credits is a preliminary proposal until the course has been approved.
